records.name: All-Or-Nothing Failure
records.definition: Failing the entire system when one part fails instead of degrading to reduced but working service.

records.name: Brittle Architecture
records.definition: A fragile design that breaks entirely under any condition it was not explicitly built for.

records.name: Exception Swallowing

distinctFrom.reason: Exception swallowing discards a real failure, while exception control flow uses exceptions for cases that are not failures.

records.definition: Catching an exception and silently discarding it, hiding the failure from callers and logs.

records.name: Fail Open
records.definition: Granting access or continuing when a security check fails, exposing the system on error.

records.name: Failure Propagation
records.definition: Letting a failure spread unchecked across component boundaries instead of containing it.

records.name: Fragile Parsing
records.definition: Parsing input so rigidly that any minor deviation causes a failure.

records.name: Non-Idempotent Operation
records.definition: An operation whose repetition changes the result, making it unsafe to retry.

records.name: Shared Resource Pool
records.definition: Serving all work from one shared resource pool, so one overloaded consumer starves the rest.

records.name: Single Behavior Path
records.definition: Providing only one execution path with no fallback, so any failure in it fails the whole request.

records.name: Trusting Invalid Inputs
records.definition: Assuming inputs are valid and using them without checking, so bad data flows through unguarded.

records.name: Unbounded Retry

distinctFrom.reason: Unbounded retry is one caller retrying with no limit, while a retry storm is many callers whose combined retries prolong the failure, bounded or not.

records.definition: Retrying a failing operation endlessly with no limit, amplifying load and delaying recovery.

records.name: Unsafe Default Continuation
records.definition: Continuing in an unsafe default state after a failure instead of stopping in a safe one.

records.name: Blast-Radius Reduction
records.definition: The ability to contain a failure so it affects only one isolated partition.

records.name: Bounded Waiting
records.definition: The ability to guarantee an operation waits no longer than a set limit.

records.name: Cascading Failure Prevention
records.definition: The ability to stop one component's failure from cascading through its callers.

records.name: Continued Operation Under Failure
records.definition: The ability to keep operating correctly despite the failure of some components.

records.name: Controlled Failure
records.definition: The ability to fail in a defined, handled way rather than crashing unpredictably.

records.name: Deny-by-Default Behavior
records.definition: The ability to default to denying access when a security check cannot complete.

records.name: Early Defect Detection
records.definition: The ability to surface a defect immediately at its source rather than letting it propagate.

records.name: Localized Recovery
records.definition: The ability to recover from a failure within its boundary without restarting the whole system.

records.name: Overload Protection
records.definition: The ability to protect a system from being overwhelmed by shedding or slowing incoming load.

records.name: Safe Failure
records.definition: The ability to fail without corrupting state or causing further damage.

records.name: Stability Under Stress
records.definition: The ability to keep functioning under load spikes and adverse conditions.

records.name: Transient Failure Recovery
records.definition: The ability to recover from short-lived failures by retrying the operation.

records.name: Backoff
records.definition: Progressively increasing the wait between retries to avoid overwhelming a recovering dependency.

records.name: Error Model
records.definition: A structured representation of the kinds of errors a system can raise and how they are categorized.

records.name: Alternate Behavior
records.definition: The requirement that a defined alternate behavior exist to use when the primary path fails.

records.name: Capacity Signaling
records.definition: The requirement that downstream capacity be signaled upstream so producers adjust their rate.

records.name: Failure Isolation
records.definition: The requirement that a failure be contained within a boundary so it cannot spread.

records.name: Failure Threshold
records.definition: The requirement of a defined failure count or rate at which a circuit breaker trips.

records.name: Feature Isolation
records.definition: The requirement that individual features be isolated so one can be disabled without taking down others.

records.name: Resource Isolation
records.definition: The requirement that resources be partitioned so exhaustion in one pool cannot starve others.

records.name: Strict Output

distinctFrom.reason: Strict output governs what a component emits, while tolerant input governs what it accepts.

records.definition: The requirement that a component emit only strictly conformant, well-formed output.

records.name: Timeout
records.definition: The requirement that an operation be given a maximum time to complete before being abandoned.

records.name: Tolerant Input
records.definition: The requirement that a component accept and cope with input that deviates from the ideal format.

records.name: Availability of Degraded Dependency
records.definition: The degree to which tripping a breaker to protect the system also cuts off a still-partly-working dependency.

records.name: Consistency / Feature Completeness
records.definition: The degree to which serving reduced functionality during failure sacrifices full consistency or completeness.

records.name: Hidden Errors
records.definition: The degree to which catching failures at a boundary can obscure the underlying errors from view.

records.name: Load Amplification
records.definition: The degree to which retrying failed operations multiplies load on an already-struggling dependency.

records.name: Slow Operation Tolerance
records.definition: The degree to which enforcing timeouts sacrifices tolerance for legitimately slow operations.

records.name: Stability
records.definition: The degree to which a system keeps operating steadily without collapsing under load.

records.name: Stale/Reduced Results
records.definition: The degree to which serving a fallback yields stale or reduced-quality results.

records.name: Strict Validation
records.definition: The degree to which rejecting deviant input conflicts with accepting it tolerantly.

records.name: Verbosity
records.definition: The degree to which pervasive defensive checks add verbosity and clutter to the code.

records.name: Introduce Typed Result
records.definition: A technique for returning success or a typed error as a value, so callers handle failure through the type system.

records.name: Translate Errors at the Boundary
records.definition: A technique for converting vendor and infrastructure errors into the core's own error types where they enter.

records.name: Idempotency Key
records.definition: A technique for tagging each request with a unique key, so a repeated request is recognized and applied once.

records.name: Bounded Retry
records.definition: A technique for retrying a failed call a limited number of times with growing delays before giving up.

records.name: Jitter
records.definition: A technique for adding a random offset to retry delays, so clients that failed together do not retry together.

records.name: Deadline Propagation
records.definition: A technique for passing the time left for a request to every call it makes, so downstream work stops when the caller has given up.

records.name: Cancellation
records.definition: A technique for letting a caller stop work it no longer needs, releasing the resources that work holds.

records.name: Load Shedding
records.definition: A technique for refusing part of the incoming work when load passes capacity, so the work already accepted completes.

records.name: Bounded Queue
records.definition: A technique for giving a queue a fixed capacity, so producers are slowed or refused instead of exhausting memory.

records.name: Fail Fast or Fall Back
records.definition: A technique for deciding per failure whether to stop with an error at once or to continue on a declared fallback.
